I feel like I'm being misunderstood here.

I don't at all feel like "beating things up" should be the default solution to a scenario, but when it's presented as an option, it should work.  This is why I feel like the starter kit's treatment of NPC's is bizarrely inconsistent:

  • Proletariat is almost entirely a non-threat.  You get him to absorb his hundreds of clones and he's wiped out, clearly no threat and not aggressive.  Yet stats are presented for him as a villain; moreover, those stats make him practically indestructible.  He shouldn't even have stats (so that the GM can adjudicate the conflict some other way), but if he does, they should make sense--he should either be beatable, or it should describe him in such a way that the fight will end in a satisfactory way without him being technically beaten.  As written, if the heroes attack him for some reason, it's virtually guaranteed that they will fail the adventure (probably by the scene tracker running out).
  • Haka, on the other hand, is an active threat.  She's strongly inclined to attack Tempest and the heroes, and attempting to subdue her forcefully is a reasonable approach.  However, talking her down is presented as the only solution.  There are no stats for her.
  • Same goes for Fanatic: She's being an active aggressor, clearly not in her right mind, swinging around that blood magic sword and generally making things worse, and a player might very reasonably try to restrain or even incapacitate her.  Again, talking her down is described as a requirement for successful completion of the scenario.

Similarly, I don't mind when an objective is significantly open-ended.  "Pinpoint the VoidHeart" is fine as it is.  Tachyon might scan for energy anomalies, Unity could create a swarm of drones to search in all directions, Legacy could focus on his Danger Sense and try to feel out which direction the greatest danger is in, Bunker or AZ could uses sensors in their suits' HUDs, etc., etc.  The book even gives some general examples in a sidebar.  And only one check from the whole team is needed.  That one is great!

Conversely, "The Signal" is awful.  It's a very constrained challenge that focuses on an entirely technological feature.  Players of heroes without science or tech abilities will be hard-pressed to find a solution to this one even thinking outside the box.  And it requires three Overcome actions, which in many games means that one player will be sitting there making all the rolls while the others sit on their heels.  It's all very well to say "if your players take a different approach, go with it," and certainly they should be allowed to do so, but if you're going to write up a whole scene that presupposes only one solution that may not make sense for many groups, you may as well write nothing and just tell the GM to improvise the whole thing.

Next point: the issues having clues that point to Baron Blade.  I read them.  I don't see it.  All the new tech is designed specfically in a way as to disguise who built it.  All the old tech is, well, old.  Even if Blade had nothing to do with any of this, an adventure in Insula Primalis would involve the heroes getting shot at by rusty old cannons that Blade left there.  Same goes for the reactor: just because Blade was involved in its design decades ago doesn't mean he has anything to do with the plot at hand.  And none of the rest of it his consistent with his style.  His tech in the card game has all either been the form of over-the-top megalomaniac stuff (doomsday devices, giant floating platforms) or personal enhancement or defense.  He built the one decoy bot of himself.  Otherwise, making robot spiders and mummies and deliberately hiding his hand in their design isn't his M.O. at all, nor his handing off some of his tech to some other random villain to use in their own scheme.

And about the rules about invoking Issues: I have read these rules as well.  Players can invoke Collections, not Issues.  There's no rule suggesting they can do what the scenario suggests, since the events haven't been compiled into a Collection yet.  Would it be reasonable to allow them to invoke an Issue instead?  Sure!  Do the rules suggest they might be able to do such a thing or how it would work?  No.  Same thing with allowing them to use Hero Points to accomplish things other than get bonuses: it's reasonable, but a player who's trying to play the game by reading the rules will never think of doing this.  The only way these things will happen is if the GM says, "Oh, by the way, here's a new rule six issues in that you can use in this situation."  This sort of thing happens when the developer writes the scenarios: they know what they generally had in mind when they wrote the rules, but they didn't actually write down the part of it that makes these situations work.

I guess the main problem I have is that if someone tries to run the adventures exactly as written, they will probably fail.  It's all fixable, by the GM adding some information here, tweaking some numbers there, and frequently by players coming up with something unanticipated that makes total sense, but none of that should be necessary.  An inexperienced GM, perhaps one who's so overwhelmed by a new system that they're having trouble improvising, or one who just isn't creative, or one who's used to adventure modules (like, yes, D&D) that attempt to cover all possible bases, might struggle with this.

On the other hand, an GM like Jeysie, experienced or not, who is wonderfully creative and has absolutely no qualms about taking the adventure completely off the rails if that seems like the most fun thing to do, will do just fine with adventures written this way (and I can see how D&D might be a struggle if that's your approach).

My concerns are:

  1. Adventures should, when possible, be written so that a wide range of styles can be used to experience them.  As they are, they work perfectly well for the creative, improvisational types but not so well for the by-the-book types.
  2. There are currently two Sentinels products.  Both of them are extremely by-the-book in design.  In the RPG, if Omnitron-X fights Plague Rat, the GM can and should simply rule that the robot is immune to infection.  In the card game, players should absolutely not do that.  There are pages and pages of rulings and examples that cover all the bizarre interactions between specific cards, which should be followed whenever possible.  Many Sentinels fans--though certainly far from all of them--will be coming into the RPG with a similar expectation.
  3. The most popular tabletop role-playing games in the world are still D&D and its offshoots.  If new players have experience with one such game, it's likely to be that one, and they're going to expect to be able to run games the way D&D works.  
  4. The core rulebook itself is pretty tight.  Its rules are clearly written (other than a couple of errors), the mechanics are functional, and approaching it from a very literal perspective is completely possible.  I'm still not sold on the Overcome table and how dangerous it is to attempt any sort of Overcome check that doesn't correspond to your better dice and one of your Principles, but that's a numerical tweak.  There are extensive, concrete examples for things like twists and risky actions that the players and GM can easily make use of (while also saying that being more creative is encouraged).  The adventure booklets (other than the first one, which has clearly been playtested much more) fall short here, where it's clear that if the same amount of playtesting and attention to detail had been put into them, they could have covered more of what many players are going to need.

TL;DR: It's great that the adventures work well for someone like Jeysie and her friends.  They don't work work well for me and mine, and I don't think I'm wrong in stating that there are a whole lot of Sentinels fans out there who are similar to me and mine.  And a whole lot of this stuff could have been easy fixes.

At the risk of jumping into the bonfire here, I'm going to toss in a few observations, coming from the perspective of a fellow RPG designer.

I have no issue with Proletariat having stats in the game.  In truth, I think that Haka, Tempest, Anubis, Visionary and Fanatic should all have stat blocks similar to that of Proletariat, to better delineate their mechanical abilities as NPCs.  And, given that, I think they should have been statted up as just that:  as NPCs.  NPCs don't, and shouldn't, follow the exact same format as PCs in this system, so the inclusion of their stats can and should absolutely look different than their stats as PCs in the forthcoming corebook.

There are, absolutely, points within the adventures that could stand to be more specific in the myriad approaches that players could take to succeed in a given scene.  Stats for Haka, for instance, would come in awfully handy, should the group decide to wrestle her into submission, rather than simply trying to talk her down.  Same with Fanatic in the nuclear plant.  Why couldn't Bunker simply "External Combustion" his way through the legion of Proletariats, burning them in one giant conflagration of clones, clearing the way?  While morbid, that's just a single example of a way--outside of the scenario as written--to succeed in that given encounter.  However, the text necessary to understand that Proletariat is a roadblock, not an adversary, isn't called out or made specifically noted. 

A sidebar here would have done a lot of good:  "Attacking Proletariat:  Your players, upon seeing an old foe like Proletariat, might immediately leap to the attack.  If they do, feel free to enter combat--we've included stats for Proletariat above, if you need them.  However, the mass of clones here doesn't actively attack any Hero unless they've been attacked, and really serve as more of an environmental hazard than an active enemy.  If your players do fight the clones, be sure to narrate the effects of both their attacks--which create more clones--and the fact that the other clones don't even seem to recognize they're being attacked.  Your players may, at that point, decide upon a route other than violence."  That's a single paragraph, but it could go a long way towards the insinuation that, "Hey, there's a better way to go than knives and guns here..."  But, as I'll get into below, space is at a premium...

There are, absolutely, points within the adventures that are 'railroady' in terms of their solution.  I think about the 'chase' through the Egyptian tomb/maze, which is abstracted to the point where there's an entire thread already devoted to how to run that specific scenario, much of which comes down to "handwave it all".  The end confrontation with Blade suffers from timing issues, given the constraints of the GYRO scene tracker mechanic.  

But--and this in no way is meant to be an apology for GtG or Critical Hits--we are looking at an incomplete rules-set here.  Any quickstart is exactly that; incomplete, basic rules.  It may well be--and probably is, truth be told--that the rules for "how to scale encounters, based on player number" is in the GMing chapter of the corebook.  It's not exactly the sort of thing that you, as a writer or a layout guru, try to cram into the 24 page booklet that's going in your quickstart.  It's not essential information to playing the system or running the game; yes, it's useful, but it's not critical.  It gets left out.  Same goes for things like, "how do I design a montage scene?" or "how do I structure this chase throughout the city?"  What we've been given here is a glimpse of what the game is like, a few iconic characters to examine, and a few scenarios within which to play.  No more, no less.

So when MindWanderer notes that--and I'm totally paraphrasing here, so don't come at me with misquotations--there's not enough detail here and we don't have an idea of how to manipulate these encounters to get around the railroaded authorial intent, he's right.  But he also needs to be patient, because that level of detail isn't possible in the type of product currently released.  That sort of granular information has to come in a heftier book.  To me, that argument is like cracking open the Basic Red Box D&D and asking "Well, what if I want to grapple this guy?  Where are the rules for disarm?  This is broken..."  As to the argument surrounding "There's stats there; that implies that we should fight"--that's a false association; only the GM can even see those stats.  To the players, Proletariat is as the GM presents him:  a viable foe, a mindless nuisence, a mass of writhing rubble, or somewhere in between.  Saying that the mere presence of a stat block implies him as an adversary insinuates that the GM literally isn't reading the module, only fishing for stats, which should rarely if ever be the case.

However, with Jeysie retorts with--again, totally paraphrasing; no hate towards either of you at all--well, you just need to interpret the rules as a GM and be creative...he's right.  But, with so many players reaching this RPG through the card game--some of whom have already mentioned limited to no playing or GMing experience--the new players have a right to want guidelines for HOW to be flexible and what they can offer a player:  what makes a good Twist or complication, what goes into a dynamic encounter, and what should go in a stat block.  While many of those details cannot--by necessity--go in a quickstart guide, guidance should be found here, especially if this is to be viewed as an intro-level piece.  That said, the insinuation that "What, aren't you creative enough to think on your own?" certainly hasn't endeared many to your viewpoint, despite the fact that I actually agree with nearly everything you've actively argued as a positive within the text.

 

TL;DR -- Jeysie and MindWanderer, you're both right, but you're coming at each side in a manner that accentuates the axact same fault.  Yes, there should have been more detail about how to GM in a narrative style, but that's not the sort of thing you can really put in a 24 page quickstart guide; I have no doubts that it's going to be covered much more deeply in the corebook, not that it helps now.  Yes, there are certain encounters that were dealt with in a railroad-y or an unwieldy manner; likely, that comes from the fact that with a limited page count, you can only cover so many contingencies.  No plan survives contact with the players; that's the first rule of GMing.  

Honestly, it sounds like the argument being made across the board is, "Why isn't X here?".  If every X was in the starter kit, it wouldn't be a starter kit--it'd be the corebook itself.  And yes, for an intro-level product, the starter kit should have included some additional advice on "What if your players do THIS?", but with word count at a premium, something has to go on the chopping block.  When you're trying to introduce a whole new mechanical system, explaing how powers and qualities and the like work, that doesn't always leave enough space for 'fluffy' items like GM advice.  It sucks, but it's a reality of publishing.  

I love you both, (you too, Spiff!); have a good holiday, if I don't get a chance to write back.

Warning: Massive post incoming. Apologies. :)

Having read the Starter Kit and all of this long thread, my thoughts:

MindWanderer: Your criticisms are valid. There is much that must be extrapolated if you come from the crunchier RPG systems where everything is accounted for via a rule. D&D is rife with rules, and every rule must be followed or players cry foul because that's not what the rules say, and the rules are binding! I know this from my years running 3.Xe through the RPGA back in the day, where min/maxxers and power gamers ruled the roost, and every splatbook was considered fair game. Those adventures were railroad one-track plots, where the slightest deviation from the narrative would result in disaster for the group, and the amount of wiggle room for player ingenuity was very narrow indeed. Follow the adventure plot from point A to B to C all the way through, and players were lead by the nose by the adventure being blatant in spelling out every little plot thread with great big bold signs that lit up like Christmas trees.

Great Hera, did I hate those days.

For every one truly creative player or gamemaster I encountered back then, there were easily 25 to 30 power gaming munchkins who would rather let the dice and stats do all the talking, and adventure design revolved entirely around the formulaic crunch and rules because that's what players expected to interact with. The catch phrase of "roll-players instead of role-players" applied heavily here.

I think a lot of the current RPG game experience is overshadowed by this great beast called D&D, and that any system that doesn't use rules crunch so extensively is treated as bad design instinctually instead of just another play experience.

I gave up on D&D and went in search for something better suited for telling stories. Found Savage Worlds Deluxe (a current favorite with my group and a great compromise between crunch and narrative playstyle), Fiasco (yes, there is dice rolling, but the actual game is entirely narrative driven and immensely satisfying when played with players who like telling group stories), Call of Cthulhu (The system reads a lot heavier than it plays, in that the math/crunch is all mainly handled by the players and the gamemaster is largely free to facillitate a great story), Dread (extremely unique system that is so light on crunch, yet the crunch really ratchets up the tension as the story progresses, which is super awesome if you like telling scary horror stories), Lamentations of the Flame Princess (old school fantasy plus heavy metal Twilght Zone using NSFW adult situations and themes, as well as serious weird fiction? Yes, please! Some crunch but only when really needed, since most of the material is just so out there and different from everything else on the market) and now the Sentinel Comics RPG, which I think achieves the goal of giving the players all the crunch they need to support what they want to do by forcing them to first describe what they want to do and then apply the crunch to determine how to make it happen in game mechanics.


As an experienced gamemaster, my entire goal over the years has been to find a system that allows for fun, compelling stories that involve thrilling action on the behalf of the players, with very little prep time required of me to make that story come to life. Twenty to thirty pages explaining how the mechanics work is about all I have the time and patience to read these days when it comes to a new system. If I can't explain that system to new players in 15 minutes or less, along with giving them a great theme to hook them into wanting to play the system, then that system gets shelved pretty quick. The Sentinels RPG has a great continuity from which to draw ideas, the rules are super easy to explain, and the adventures are set up to allow the gamemaster to do the same thing as the players, i.e. describe what they want to add, then use the rules crunch to make it happen in game mechanics.


Are there details that seem to be omitted? Coming from that heavy D&D crunch grognard background, the old RPGA judge/gamemaster in me is screaming right alongside MindWanderer. Who let this go to print? This is a big pile of threads and no actual details! Why give stats for something you aren't supposed to fight? The only reason for stats to be put in the adventure is for the gamemaster to run a combat encounter with them! It's so broken! Players can't possibly win! Arrghh! Gripes! Fist waving in GTG's general direction! Don't they know what they're supposed to be doing?!? Terrible design! Grrr!

But! But, that is the old way of doing things and this system seems to want to break different ground with a unique system that encourages a different way of playing. One where the players and the gamemaster are encouraged to be more creative, let go of the D&D rules safety blanket, and trust that they can create a super awesome comic book story without needing all that crunch. And no slight towards Champion, but a roleplaying game where you are a comic book superhero needs the system to be light enough to fly in order to be able to tell those super awesome comic book stories. The card game already has all the crunch for people looking for crunch. That system already exists, where you get to be a Sentinel Comics superhero and use crunchy rules to beat up the bad guy.

This RPG is a different experience than that, because eventually you will be able to create your own Sentinel Comics superhero and tell your own stories. That is something that is very difficult to do in the card game. You can do it, but that's a lot of time spent designing a deck of cards that will work within that crunchy playset.

I can understand someone coming in expecting everything to be crunchy details and guide you by the nose, but it honestly looks like Christopher and Co are trying to create something new and different from what has come before. Finding the right balance of which details are important to include in a roleplaying adventure and which are not so important appears to be a learning process right now. More than likely they will be learning a great deal from us here on the forums, and they will take MindWanderer's concerns into consideration moving forward. I don't expect they will completely rewrite the Starter Kit, but then we're talking about a company that completely overhauled the launch product that started all this back in 2011. So maybe they'll revisit it in the future? PDFs are super easy to revise and release to a customer base, given that a proper structure is put in place to allow redownloading of purchased digital content.

Anyway, I'm digressing a bit...

The adventures included in the Starter Kit are... fairly loose in presentation. Is this a bad thing? For me, as an experienced gamemaster looking for a narrative based system that isn't all about rules and crunch dictating what players can and cannot do, I don't think it is. The adventures are meant to give gamemasters new to this system something to go on, teaching how a gamemaster for Sentinel Comics RPG can run a game session. In that regard, I think they're adequate in achieving that goal. There is an inherent flaw to every published adventure out there no matter what RPG system, in that they are written with a certain playgroup in mind, and this means that every adventure by its nature and design has to be tailored and adjusted to fit your specific playgroup. I feel these adventures were written with all six of the characters intended to be used, even if one or two players has to double up to get them all in, but at the same time the very system--the crunch itself--is set up to accomodate a fluctuation in numbers, which in turn means the adventures are probably the closest to being useable straight out of the kit no matter who is playing. That's exciting to think about from a design perspective.

The missing details and the impossible stats included seem more like a tease of what's to come for a gamemaster when the full core rulebook comes out. After all, this is a product meant to get you interested in learning more about the system and what potential it has for your gaming group. Is Proletariat completely unbeatable? Maybe. But the story being told by the adventure says the point isn't to "beat" Proletariat. It's to save him. And isn't that really what being a superhero means at the very core of the idea?

Haka is meant to be impossible to beat in a fight, and at a table with six players it is hoped that someone will get the idea that fighting her isn't a good idea. But what if they don't? What if they decide this person needs to be slapped down? Well, the gamemaster has a few options. Go ahead and narrate the fight, let the players roll dice and then describe how Haka easily tosses the heroes around like rag dolls while gunning for Tempest. What's the end result here, from a story perspective? Forget rules and stats because that's not what's important to the story here. What's important is that the heroes figure out how to save Tempest before Haka beats the snot outta him, which is what happens when that scene tracker counts down to zero. I would expect a few rounds of the gamemaster not rolling anything and describing the incredible ease with which they are losing the fight to this woman who vaguely reminds them of their missing friend would be enough for the players to say, okay, this isn't working, brute force clearly isn't the right choice, time to try something else. Even going so far as to have Tempest avoiding Haka's attacks early on and trying to talk her down or explain how he doesn't know her at all might get the idea across to the heroes that this is a case of mistaken identity. Sure, the adventure doesn't spell it out and it doesn't give stats for Haka, or for Fanatic who is pretty much doing the same thing, but in examining the base crunch of the system, if it did so, then it would be robbing the gamemaster of having any impact on the story being told. And the gamemaster is just as important to the storytelling equation as the players. They should have fun too. So my take on these missing details is not one of bad design but of supporting the core design of the game, that being that everyone is trying to tell a super awesome comic book hero story. The gamemaster gets to play too, but not like in other roleplaying games where they are the keeper of the stats and crunch. Here, they can bring their own creativity to the session without it all being dictated to them by the designers.

Should there be stats for Haka and Fanatic and Tempest and all the other heroes the players encounter? Maybe, maybe not. I see it as a deliberate choice by the designers to not include them, because ultimately the session isn't about their stats. It's about the players being superheroes, and superheroes need someone to save and someone to beat up, and they need to figure out when one or the other applies in a given situation. When the heroes first encounter Proletariat by the hundreds, they're completely mindless and present no real threat. It's only when the players actually explore the plant and find out that Fanatic is the real problem here that anything can start to be resolved. When/If Proletariat recovers, he's too exhausted to fight anyone, doesn't really want to stick around, and leaves pretty much after telling the heroes he saw Baron Blade arrive at the plant. The heroes really have no reason to want to attack him when he is grateful for them rescuing him in the first place.

Fanatic is a friend to the heroes, and it should be clear to them that something is wrong with her emotionally. But let's say the heroes go into attack mode and decide they need to fight her. Well, the gamemaster could just waste a few rounds not rolling dice and having Fanatic give warnings to not get involved, like it says in the adventure. But this is another chance for the gamemaster to interact and play with the players instead of just reading stats and rolling dice. What's the ultimate story outcome here if the heroes do nothing but fight Fanatic? The plant explodes. Proletariat pops back into one body, everyone is knocked unconscious, Fanatic flies away, and the heroes don't look so good going into the next adventure. Surely the heroes will come up with a different strategy before that happens, yes?

So, now that I've written that whole novel that no one will want to read, here's where I feel the Starter Kit fails:

First, the PDFs aren't bookmarked. Being able to click page numbers in the Table of Contents to navigate the document makes for a better digital resource. Or maybe they are and I don't have the feature turned on. I don't know. But it's a super handy feature in other digital gaming resource files, so it'd be nice if that were added to future products.

Second, I played the demo at Gen Con, which consisted of the first adventure, and it was run by Philippe-Antoine Ménard, which is probably about as high up on the design chain as one can get short of having Christopher running the game. There is a key element that Phillippe-Antoine used during that demo that isn't discussed at all in the Starter Kit, and seems to me to be absolutely crucial for the players to understand what exactly they are supposed to do in a given scene.

That element is index cards. Let me explain.

Phillippe-Antoine started the game by describing the devastation in Megalopolis, then asked each of us what we wanted to do to help with the recovery efforts, specifically asking where we were in the city, and encouraging partnerships when it made sense. He would then write down the name of that location on an index card and put it out in front of us on the table. Then when the spider bots attacked, he wrote "Objective: Defeat the Spider Bots" with a check mark box next to it on another index card, and wrote "d6" for each spider bot on each location index card (3 per player). All of this told us players exactly what we needed to do, how many bots there were, and where they were located. Commence battle, where Phillipe-Antoine crossed out a "d6" every time a spider bot in that location was destroyed. Once all the spider bots were destroyed, he checked the box on the Defeat the Spider Bots card. High fives all around.

Next, Unity examined the bots and found the mixture of code. She also got high enough to merit knowing they all worked together via a particular wavelength frequency that was controlling them via a hive mind setup. Interesting information...

Players get the distress call at Akash'Flora from Argent Adept. Off the heroes zoom! Phillipe-Antoine begins laying out more index cards: "Objective: Defeat the Spider Mothership" with its "d10" marked, and telling us how it's laying eggs at a rapid rate, which are turning into harvesters that crawl onto the tree; "Objective: Find the Signal Source" with no boxes, representing the information we learned about the bots and how they are all being controlled from somewhere; "Objective: Stop the Harvesters" with no boxes, and telling us about the vast horde of bots crawling all over the tree and how there are far too many for us to pick off individually; "Objective: Rescue the Human Shields" with the -2 penalty written out, and telling us that they are being used to protect the harvesters, drawing two boxes representing the effort required to rescue some and then all of the civilians; "Objective: Defeat the Armored Spider Bot Snipers" with their "d6" numbers, and telling us how they've found strategic places to web up and offer superior tactical fire on those trying to interfere with the harvesters; "Objective: Defeat the Roaming Spider Bots" with their "d6" numbers, telling us about how there are some wandering bots acting like soldiers; and finally, "Objective: Rescue Argent Adept" adding a check box and writing "Find Argent Adept" next to it, while saying we heroes know Argent Adept is in trouble but have no idea where he is within the chaos that is happening.

As those index cards kept coming out, the enormity of the problem in front of us heroes became clear. Staring at that table top littered with all those objectives made the scene seem overwhelming. Yet one by one, we each took on a challenge and began earning checkmarks on those objectives. Unity managed to hack a spider bot, locate the transmitter on the Mothership, and even had the spider bot transform into a blinking "weak spot" identifying exactly where we needed to hit the Mothership to knock out all the spider bots in one go. As we uncovered new information in the scene, Phillipe-Antoine added check boxes, such as once Argent Adept was found and checked off, a new box was added with "Save him without further injuries" next to it. When that happened, he added the optional check box, "Stabilize him", which added to the tension of the scene as we realized we weren't sure when an objective would be entirely complete.

The index cards served a vital play experience purpose in focusing the attention of the players on what their objectives were, using language that gave a subtle clue as to what strategy would work best. In this aspect, the Starter Kit fails the new gamemaster as well as the experienced one, as I feel this element to be absolutely necessary to the play experience. It communicates a massive amount of information in a very organized fashion, and facilitates the gameplay by giving the players just enough guidance for such an open narrative system.

Just adding an index card that says "Objective: Get past the Proletariats!" or "Objective: Find Fanatic" and slowly revealing the new check boxes one by one as in saving Argent Adept above, is enough to get players into the swing of what they actually need to do. It was this element of the demo that most reminded me of the card game since it so clearly showed what was going on in the story.

Without explaining this index card element, the Starter Kit fumbles in telling a more crunchy or punchy based game group what they need to do or how to keep track of what's going on. The game can be played without this index card element and the solutions could be happened upon more narratively, but I wouldn't recommend it starting out unless you have a group that can handle that much freedom. For a first time experience of the system, with the Starter Kit as the only exposure to the game, then not having this index card element makes the game more challenging to run and play overall, and can lead to a lot of the frustration as expressed by MindWanderer as regards "What if my group just wants to fight everything?" With the index card element there with a check box that says, "Talk down Fanatic from her murderous rage" or something similar, the group will start understanding that punching everything isn't the only answer, and that in turn can help inform your choice of words when filling out the index cards in future encounters. You could use "Talk down" or just use exactly what's listed in the adventure--"Get Fanatic to stop fighting long enough to actually listen to you".

When I start to look at the adventures with the index card element in mind, everything falls into place for me. I get what the creators are trying to accomplish and why the adventures are written the way they are. That this element is not discussed or shown in the Gameplay Guide nor in any of the adventures is puzzling to me as it feels so integral to the experience and how to actually run the adventures. It could be one of those "little details" that is so insidious in the design and playtest phase that it was hiding in plain sight so to speak, and it was just taken for granted that it would be understood without needing to explain it. Or maybe that's how they found to best run the game and figured it was just a gamemaster trick to help run it and did not actually consider it a part of the system. I can't really imagine playing the Starter Kit without it, nor could I imagine a gamemaster designing their own scenes without using it.

So yeah. Index cards. Use 'em. The entire kit cleans up a bunch when you do. :)

Don't dismiss or belittle those who may be struggling on that curve. And if you don't see the curve, then at least accept the fact that your perception is not the only valid one and that you may not be best suited at addressing their issues.

Some off the top of my head of what I was trying to say more or less this entire time:

  1. I feel like the system takes a lot of things me and my group struggled with during our time playing D&D and makes an attempt to fix them. It looks like it does a good job of that, though that comes from reading through it and not getting to play it yet.

  2. The game system is definitely geared more towards the freeform side of things despite having a fair bit more crunch than the average freeform game. I agree therefore with the idea that freeform players will probably have an easier time sliding in (since the dice system looks pretty simple), while crunch players will have to adjust their mindsets more significantly if they want to give it a go.

As someone with a sort of hybrid group which was often trying to do a lot of narrative in the d20 system yet was too wary of trying to adjucate via fiat rather than dice, I can see how this system could address a lot of the issues we had with combat, though conversely having our skill-heavy play be condensed into Overcome checks + narrative would still require some mindset switching.

  1. Considering having to think up an overall structured plot and tons of stats on the fly was a big chunk of why my attempt to GM went south, I can see how this adventure and system would do a lot to solve those areas I struggled with.

  2. To follow from that, this system seems to be a lot more forgiving any time you need to wing it, because it's already a lot more ad hoc to begin with, and speaking as my own not-that-great-at-being-creative self, I feel "winging it" is by far the hardest skill to acquire as a GM, so I feel anything that helps with that is a huge plus.

Edit:

And I will also be fair to everyone who wants me to look at MindWanderer's POV and I will say it seems boil down to an issue of clashing axioms.

MindWanderer seems to RP with a pretty by-the-book group whose creativity falls within a definite finite and reasonable set of parameters.

My RP experience in the past thus far has been with a group that was, to put it straightforwardly, a bunch of eccentric oddballs.

So MindWanderer seems to have strong expectations of an adventure and system that accounts for every reasonable variable choice/outcome and docks heavily for adventures and systems that don't provide that. Conversely they put little to no real value on the ability to ad hoc because they rarely need it.

Meanwhile, I am fairly certain nothing short of a quantum-level AI could anticipate what my group could come up with, so I don't place as much priority on an adventure accounting for everything in detail so long as it gives a good outline and a general idea of what needs to happen and some general ideas on ways to get back on track if it doesn't. Conversely, I value strongly and grant points for any system that makes dealing with unexpected things on the fly easier to do.

So we were stuck because they're criticizing how the adventure doesn't give enough detail for what their group needs, and I was saying how I think the adventure gives enough detail for my group's needs considering we're probably just going to do something totally weird anyway and so more relevantly to us it also gives enough flexibility for what my group needs.

We were also stuck in that they were like, "It's unreasonable to expect a GM to ever need to paper over anything" and I was like "It's unreasonable to expect that a GM will never need to paper over anything" because we are both right considering our own personal experiences.

So hooray for "competing access needs", as some of the jargon goes.
